title: China Confirms Xi to Visit India for First Time in Seven Years
excerpt: President Xi Jinping will attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12–13, with bilateral talks and a trade-minister meeting set amid record trade and a record deficit.
body:
• China announced on September 10 that President Xi Jinping will attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12–13, his first visit to India in nearly seven years.
  • Trade ministers Wang Wentao and Piyush Goyal are expected to hold talks on the sidelines, with India seeking easing of export controls and China pressing for relaxed investment restrictions.
  • Bilateral trade reached $91.72 billion in the first half of the year, up 23.6%, but India's deficit hit $67.1 billion and is on track to break last year's record $116.12 billion.
  • The diplomatic thaw continues after the 2024 Kazan meeting, yet analysts say deep mistrust over investment curbs, visa delays and stalled equipment shipments leaves business ties lagging far behind.

Beijing confirmed on Thursday that Chinese President Xi Jinping will travel to New Delhi for the annual BRICS summit on September 12 and 13, marking his first visit to India since an informal summit with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Mamallapuram in October 2019.

The announcement, reported by The Hindu, sets up a closely watched bilateral meeting between Xi and Modi on the summit's sidelines, along with a separate trade-focused sit-down between Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal. Wang Yi, China's foreign minister and a Politburo member, will accompany Xi as part of a large delegation.

Context & Background

The seven-year gap in top-level visits reflects the deep freeze that followed the Galwan Valley clash of June 2020, the worst violence along the disputed border in decades. Relations began a gradual normalisation after Modi and Xi met in October 2024 on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in Kazan, and momentum carried into an SCO summit meeting in Tianjin in August 2025, where both sides said their countries were "development partners and not rivals."

Last month, the two countries agreed to advance discussions on "an early and substantial harvest of boundary delimitation" after the 25th round of Special Representatives talks in Beijing, and added two new military hotlines in the Eastern and Middle sectors of the border. But tensions have flared in Arunachal Pradesh in recent weeks, with a standoff reported near Taksing in Upper Subansiri district and a first Corps Commander-level meeting for the Eastern Sector held on September 6.

Impact & Analysis

Trade will dominate the economic agenda. Two-way bilateral trade hit $91.72 billion in the first half of 2026, a 23.6% rise from last year, and is on track to surpass the record $155.62 billion figure of 2025, when China was again India's largest goods trading partner. But India's deficit reached $67.1 billion in the same period — already more than half of last year's record $116.12 billion — and the composition of trade, heavy on finished electronics and equipment, troubles New Delhi more than the headline number.

The trade minister talks are expected to air both sides' grievances: India wants Beijing to ease export controls that have held up solar panels, electronics components and even tunnel-boring machines at Chinese customs, while China wants India to relax the investment restrictions imposed after the 2020 clashes, according to The Hindu. A Reuters analysis of the visit found business ties lagging diplomacy badly — New Delhi recently declined to link Alipay to India's instant payments system on national security grounds, is weighing an investigation into Xiaomi over alleged irregularities, and has seen Indian businesspeople face fresh visa trouble, while Beijing has restricted sales of critical technology to India.

"China certainly wants to improve ties, but we are waiting to see to what extent India is actually willing to improve them."

— Lin Minwang, Fudan University

Hu Shisheng, director of the South Asia Institute at the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, described the dynamic as "strategic risk management rather than strategic realignment," telling The Hindu that both sides are building "a more stable form of competitive coexistence" — keeping the border peaceful and restoring practical cooperation without pretending strategic competition has disappeared.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian-American and global Indian business communities, the visit matters in practical terms. India's easing of Chinese investment rules in March — targeted at electronics, capital goods and solar cells — has already produced joint ventures like the Dixon Technologies–Vivo manufacturing deal, and a productive summit could open more space for Indian diaspora professionals working across supply chains, technology and trade finance. The reverse is equally true: stalled equipment shipments and visa friction are exactly the kind of business uncertainty that diaspora investors watch closely.

What's Next

The test comes this weekend. A substantive Modi–Xi bilateral and the Goyal–Wang Wentao trade discussion could unlock movement on export controls and investment rules; a ceremonial summit would confirm analysts' scepticism that the thaw remains diplomatic rather than economic. India's Ambassador to China, Vikram Doraiswami, wrote in the Global Times on Thursday that "peace and tranquility in the China-India border areas provide an essential foundation for this partnership" — a reminder that the 3,488-km Line of Actual Control still sets the ceiling on everything else.
nri_angle: Indian-American and global Indian business professionals face practical stakes in the visit, from supply-chain and investment rules to visas and trade finance.
